newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria oil export staff play down strike threat.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria oil export staff play down strike threat.

text.p: Union leaders at the Department of Petroleum Resources (DPR), which processes export documents for oil shipments by Nigeria, said on Thursday they had not yet taken a decision to go on strike from Friday over their salary arrears.

"We will be having an emergency meeting on Monday to discuss this issue with a view to taking the final decision," Victor Ajakaye, chairman of the DPR chapter of the white-collar oil workers' union PENGASSAN told Reuters.
His counterpart of the blue-collar union NUPENG, Patrick Emordi, said: "For now we have not thought of strike because we hope to dialogue with the petroleum minister."
Oil prices rose on Tuesday on news that the 3,000-strong DPR staff, who are owed salaries for January and February, had threatened to go on strike if they were not paid by Friday.
"I can't really say now that we will go on strike, that will depend on what happens in the next few days," Ajakaye said.
He said staff were unhappy over the pay situation and this had heightened tension at several locations.

DPR staff have generally been disgruntled since last summer when the Nigerian military government contracted outside inspectors to check oil shipments following allegations that tankers were being overloaded without the government receiving the extra revenue.

But the oil unions have been powerless to force a showdown since 1994, when the military government sacked and detained their key leaders because of a two-month strike in support of presidential claimant Moshood Abiola.
"If by the second week of March we don't get up to date payment of our salaries and all other benefits we will address our members on the necessary action to take," said NUPENG's Emordi.
"Let the government interprete what such action will be," he added.
The union executives said a strike by their members would disrupt Nigeria's oil exports.
"Since we are the ones doing the documentation at the terminals any action by us will certainly slow down loading," said Ajakaye.
